p48: 48.  The above paragraphs apply in so far as they comply with the Hague Convention and Council of the European Union Regulation (EC) No 2201/2003.
p49: 49.  Section 61B of that Act defines parental responsibility as “all the duties, powers, responsibilities and authority which, by law, parents have in relation to children”.
p50: 50.  Section 61C provides that each of the parents of a child who is not 18 has parental responsibility for the child, subject to any court orders.
p52: 52.  Before the Grand Chamber the applicant alleged that, as a result of the Latvian courts’ decision to order her daughter’s return to Australia, she had been the victim of an infringement of her right to respect for her family life within the meaning of Article 8 of the Convention, which reads as follows:
p53: 53.  The Grand Chamber notes that, in the proceedings before it, the Government expressly stated that they did not dispute that the Latvian courts’ decisions ordering the applicant to return E. to Australia amounted to an interference with her right to respect for her family life as protected by Article 8 of the Convention.
p54: 54.  The interference with the applicant’s right to respect for her private and family life noted above will breach Article 8 unless it satisfies the requirements of paragraph 2 of that provision. It therefore remains to be determined whether it was “in accordance with the law”, pursued one or more of the legitimate aims set out in that paragraph and was “necessary in a democratic society” in order to achieve them.
p55: 55.  The Chamber held that the rules deriving from domestic law and the Hague Convention indicated with sufficient clarity that, in order to determine whether or not the removal had been wrongful within the meaning of Article 3 of the Hague Convention, the Latvian courts had to ascertain whether the removal had been in breach of rights of custody as attributed under Australian law, Australia being the State in which the child had been habitually resident immediately before her removal. While noting that the Australian authorities had ruled on T.’s parental responsibility after the child’s removal, it observed that it had merely been confirmed, and not established, that the applicant and T. had had joint parental responsibility for the child since her birth by virtue of the Australian Family Law Act. The Chamber further found that the applicant had not been prevented from participating in the proceedings in Australia that had led to that decision, or from appealing, and, moreover, that she had not contested before the domestic courts the evidence adduced to prove that T. was the child’s father. The Chamber presumed that the decision given on 19 November 2008 by the Latvian court ordering the child’s return to Australia, which had become enforceable on 26 January 2009, had been in accordance with the law within the meaning of Article 8 of the Convention.
p56: 56.  Before the Chamber the applicant submitted that the domestic court had not been entitled to apply the provisions of the Hague Convention, since she had been raising her daughter alone at the time of her departure for Latvia. She did not comment on this point before the Grand Chamber.
p57: 57.  The Government submitted that the interference had indisputably been “in accordance with the law”, since it had been based on the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction.
